title: The Steel Box That Shrunk the World

passage.title: The Steel Box That Shrunk the World
passage.author: BEACON Assessment Lab
passage.text:
For hundreds of years, loading an ocean cargo ship was slow, hard work. Dock crews had to carry wooden barrels, cloth sacks of coffee, and loose crates up narrow gangplanks one piece at a time. Once inside the dark ship hold, workers spent days wedging every odd-shaped bundle tight so the load would not shift in rough seas. Because this step took so long, freight ships often sat tied to piers for weeks. The port dock itself had become a costly bottleneck for world trade.

In the 1950s, a former trucking owner named Malcom McLean watched dockworkers hoist single cotton bales onto a ship in New York. He saw that unpacking a truck just to repack a ship wasted huge amounts of time and money. What if the whole steel trailer box could be lifted off the truck wheels? Then it could be stacked right onto a ship. When the box reached the next port, a crane could set it onto a waiting train car or truck frame. No one would have to touch the goods inside.

On April 26, 1956, McLean tested his bold idea on a refitted oil tanker named the Ideal X. Fifty-eight large metal boxes, packed with loose factory goods by warehouse crews in New Jersey, were smoothly hoisted onto the ship deck by a giant dock crane. Cranes loaded the whole ship in less than eight hours instead of a full week. Six days later, the ship docked in Houston, Texas. Waiting trucks hauled the sealed boxes straight to stores. The cost of loading freight dropped from nearly six dollars a ton to just sixteen cents a ton.

For this system to work across the globe, however, every shipping company had to agree on uniform box sizes and corner locks. If one port used ten-foot hooks while another used twelve-foot clamps, cranes could not lift boxes from foreign ships. In the 1960s, trade groups set strict rules for twenty-foot and forty-foot steel boxes. Every box had matching corner locks. Soon, any crane in Tokyo, Rotterdam, or Savannah could lift any box in the world.

Today, vast container ships carry up to twenty thousand steel boxes across the sea on a single trip. Goods made in distant plants move smoothly from ship to train to truck in locked steel boxes. By turning messy piles of freight into neat building blocks, the simple shipping container reshaped how the modern world buys and sells almost everything.

tier2Words.definition: Goods and products carried by a ship, train, plane, or truck

tier2Words.definition: A narrow or slow point in a system that holds up everything else
tier2Words.rootHint: bottle + neck (the narrow top of a bottle where liquid pours out slowly)

tier2Words.contextClue: Contrasted with 'If one port used ten-foot hooks while another used twelve-foot clamps.'

tier2Words.contextClue: Modern container ships 'carry up to twenty thousand steel boxes across the sea on a single trip.'

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"Fifty-eight large metal boxes, packed with loose factory goods by warehouse crews in New Jersey, were smoothly hoisted onto the ship deck by a giant dock crane."

In the main clause of this sentence, who or what hoisted the fifty-eight large metal boxes onto the ship deck?

options.text: The warehouse crews working in New Jersey
options.diagnosticNote: Confuses the agent inside the middle participial phrase ('packed... by warehouse crews') with the agent of the main verb ('were smoothly hoisted').
options.childFeedback: Careful—this choice confuses the noun inside the middle describing phrase ('packed... by warehouse crews') with who or what actually did the main action ('were smoothly hoisted').

options.text: A giant dock crane at the port
options.diagnosticNote: Correctly identifies the passive agent following the main verb ('were smoothly hoisted onto the ship deck by a giant dock crane').
options.childFeedback: Spot on! This answer correctly identifies the doer of the action following the main verb ('were smoothly hoisted onto the ship deck by a giant dock crane').

options.text: The loose factory goods inside the containers
options.diagnosticNote: Selects a noun phrase inside the embedded modifier rather than the machine that lifted the boxes.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—this choice selects a noun phrase inside the middle describing phrase rather than the machine that lifted the boxes.

options.text: The fifty-eight large metal boxes on the pier
options.diagnosticNote: Confuses the grammatical subject/receiver of the passive verb ('Fifty-eight large metal boxes') with the actor performing the lifting.
options.childFeedback: Careful—this choice confuses the subject receiving the action ('Fifty-eight large metal boxes') with the actor performing the lifting.

questions.provingSentenceText: Fifty-eight large metal boxes, packed with loose factory goods by warehouse crews in New Jersey, were smoothly hoisted onto the ship deck by a giant dock crane.
questions.childTip: Spot on! This answer correctly identifies the doer of the action following the main verb ('were smoothly hoisted onto the ship deck by a giant dock crane').
questions.parentExplanation: Sentence Surgery (ELAGSE5L1) with a double-'by' passive trap. Warehouse crews packed the goods, but 'a giant dock crane' performed the main action ('were smoothly hoisted').
questions.retryHint: In Paragraph 3, look for the main verb 'were smoothly hoisted.' Which 'by' phrase comes after that verb to tell what lifted the boxes?

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"For this system to work across the globe, however, every shipping company had to agree on uniform box sizes and corner locks."

What does the word uniform mean as it is used in the sentence?

options.text: Odd-shaped and different at every single port
options.diagnosticNote: Gives the exact opposite meaning; different hook and box sizes prevented cranes from lifting foreign containers.
options.childFeedback: Not quite—this choice gives the exact opposite meaning; different hook and box sizes prevented cranes from lifting foreign containers.

options.text: Special work clothes worn by ship captains
options.diagnosticNote: Selects the common noun meaning of 'uniform' (clothing) instead of the adjective meaning ('uniform box sizes').
options.childFeedback: Watch out—this choice selects the common noun meaning of 'uniform' (clothing) instead of the adjective meaning ('uniform box sizes').

options.text: Standard and matching in size and shape
options.diagnosticNote: Uses the root 'uni- + form' (one shape) and the surrounding context of matching twenty-foot and forty-foot sizes with matching corner locks.
options.childFeedback: Spot on! This answer uses the root 'uni- + form' (one shape) and the surrounding context of matching twenty-foot and forty-foot sizes with matching corner locks.

options.text: Built out of lightweight wooden barrels and cloth sacks
options.diagnosticNote: Confuses modern standardized steel containers with the old break-bulk barrels and sacks in Paragraph 1.
options.childFeedback: Careful—this choice confuses modern standardized steel containers with the old break-bulk barrels and sacks in Paragraph 1.

questions.provingSentenceText: For this system to work across the globe, however, every shipping company had to agree on uniform box sizes and corner locks.
questions.childTip: Spot on! This answer uses the root 'uni- + form' (one shape) and the surrounding context of matching twenty-foot and forty-foot sizes with matching corner locks.
questions.parentExplanation: Multiple-Meaning & Morphological Vocabulary (ELAGSE5RI4/L4). Here 'uniform' is an adjective modifying 'box sizes and corner locks,' meaning having one standard, matching form.
questions.retryHint: In Paragraph 4, look at the word parts 'uni-' (one) and 'form' (shape), and check why cranes in Tokyo and Savannah needed boxes to match.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 1, why did freight ships before the 1950s often have to sit tied to port piers for weeks?

options.text: Workers had to carry loose barrels, sacks, and crates aboard one by one and wedge each odd-shaped bundle tight by hand.
options.diagnosticNote: Accurately traces the cause-and-effect chain in Paragraph 1 explaining why manual loading and stowing took so long.
options.childFeedback: Spot on! This answer accurately traces the cause-and-effect chain in Paragraph 1 explaining why manual loading and stowing took so long.

options.text: Giant dock cranes broke down every day because twenty-foot steel containers were too heavy to lift.
options.diagnosticNote: Anachronistically mixes 1960s steel containers into the pre-1950s era described in Paragraph 1.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—this choice mistakenly mixes 1960s steel containers into the pre-1950s era described in Paragraph 1.

options.text: Ships had to wait for ocean storms to pass because wooden barrels floated away in rough seas.
options.diagnosticNote: Misuses the phrase 'rough seas' from Paragraph 1; workers wedged bundles tight inside the hold for rough seas.
options.childFeedback: Careful—this choice misuses the phrase 'rough seas' from Paragraph 1; workers wedged bundles tight inside the hold for rough seas.

options.text: Port laws banned any ship from leaving harbor until its crew had rested for thirty days.
options.diagnosticNote: Invents a port law about thirty-day rests not mentioned in the text.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—this choice invents a port law about thirty-day rests not mentioned in the text.

questions.provingSentenceText: Once inside the dark ship hold, workers spent days wedging every odd-shaped bundle tight so the load would not shift in rough seas.
questions.childTip: Spot on! This answer accurately traces the cause-and-effect chain in Paragraph 1 explaining why manual loading and stowing took so long.
questions.parentExplanation: Click-to-Prove Cause and Effect (ELAGSE5RI3). Paragraph 1 shows that carrying loose items up gangplanks and wedging odd-shaped bundles by hand caused ships to sit in port for weeks.
questions.retryHint: Look in Paragraph 1 for the sentence that explains what workers spent days doing inside the dark ship hold.

questions.prompt: In Paragraph 3, the author claims that Malcom McLean's container system saved huge amounts of time and money on its very first voyage. Which evidence from Paragraph 3 best supports this claim?

options.text: The Ideal X was a refitted oil tanker that sailed from New Jersey to Houston, Texas, on April 26, 1956.
options.diagnosticNote: States background facts about the ship's name, route, and date, but does not prove time or money savings.
options.childFeedback: Not quite—this choice states background facts about the ship's name, route, and date, but does not prove time or money savings.

options.text: Cranes loaded the ship in eight hours instead of a week, and loading costs fell to sixteen cents a ton.
options.diagnosticNote: Directly proves both parts of the claim with specific time data (eight hours vs. a week) and cost data ($6.00 vs. $0.16 per ton).
options.childFeedback: Spot on! This answer directly proves both parts of the claim with specific time data (eight hours vs. a week) and cost data ($6.00 vs. $0.16 per ton).

options.text: Warehouse crews in New Jersey packed loose factory goods inside the fifty-eight large metal boxes.
options.diagnosticNote: Describes what was inside the boxes rather than providing evidence of faster loading or lower costs.
options.childFeedback: Not quite—this choice describes what was inside the boxes rather than providing evidence of faster loading or lower costs.

options.text: Every ship in the world immediately stopped carrying cotton bales on April 26, 1956.
options.diagnosticNote: Uses extreme language ('Every ship in the world immediately stopped') unsupported by the text.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—this choice uses extreme language ('Every ship in the world immediately stopped') unsupported by the text.

questions.provingSentenceText: The cost of loading freight dropped from nearly six dollars a ton to just sixteen cents a ton.
questions.childTip: Spot on! This answer directly proves both parts of the claim with specific time data (eight hours vs. a week) and cost data ($6.00 vs. $0.16 per ton).
questions.parentExplanation: Focus standard ELAGSE5RI8 (Author's Claims & Supporting Evidence). To support the claim that containerization saved both time and money, the author provides concrete before-and-after metrics in Paragraph 3: loading time fell from a week to under 8 hours, and cost per ton fell from ~$6.00 to 16 cents.
questions.retryHint: Look for the exact numbers in Paragraph 3 that prove how much time and money the Ideal X saved.

questions.prompt: PART A: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?

options.text: Malcom McLean bought an old oil tanker named the Ideal X because he wanted to ship oil from New Jersey to Texas.
options.diagnosticNote: Misinterprets why McLean used a refitted oil tanker in Paragraph 3.
options.childFeedback: Careful—this choice misinterprets why McLean used a refitted oil tanker in Paragraph 3.

options.text: Dockworkers in the 1800s preferred carrying cloth sacks of coffee up narrow gangplanks because cranes had not been invented yet.
options.diagnosticNote: Focuses only on a minor historical detail from Paragraph 1.
options.childFeedback: Not quite—this choice focuses only on a minor historical detail from Paragraph 1.

options.text: Standardized steel shipping containers transformed global trade by allowing cargo to move quickly and cheaply between ships, trains, and trucks without being unpacked.
options.diagnosticNote: Synthesizes the problem (slow manual ports), McLean's intermodal invention, global standardization, and modern trade impact.
options.childFeedback: Spot on! This answer brings together the problem (slow manual ports), McLean's intermodal invention, global standardization, and modern trade impact.

options.text: Ports in Tokyo, Rotterdam, and Savannah are the only harbors in the world deep enough to hold container ships.
options.diagnosticNote: Turns three example ports from Paragraph 4 into an extreme, inaccurate restriction ('the only harbors').
options.childFeedback: Watch out—this choice turns three example ports from Paragraph 4 into an extreme, inaccurate restriction ('the only harbors').

questions.provingSentenceText: By turning messy piles of freight into neat building blocks, the simple shipping container reshaped how the modern world buys and sells almost everything.
questions.childTip: Spot on! This answer brings together the problem (slow manual ports), McLean's intermodal invention, global standardization, and modern trade impact.
questions.parentExplanation: Part A of the EBSR pair tests Central Idea synthesis (ELAGSE5RI2). Option C integrates McLean's innovation, global standardization, and the transformation of world trade.
questions.retryHint: In Paragraphs 1 to 5, choose the big idea that explains how standard steel containers changed shipping across the whole world.
